21.title: Medical Physics Applications in the Health Sector
21.assignments: Up to two assignments. Assignment 1 covers learning aims A and B (non-ionising and ionising techniques for diagnosis and treatment, AB.D1), usually a case-study report. Assignment 2 covers learning aim C (risks, side effects and safety precautions, C.D2 and C.D3).
21.bigIdea: Every technique is a trade-off: what it shows or treats, how the physics makes that possible, and what it costs the service user and the operator in risk. Distinction work keeps one service user at the centre and lets the physics drive the recommendation.
evidence: Anchor everything to your case-study service user: their condition, age, medical history, implants, pregnancy status.
For every technique, link principle and production (e.g. hydrogen nuclei resonance and relaxation in MRI) to what the image or treatment can and cannot do.
Use comparison tables and annotated diagrams, but follow every table with written judgement - a table alone is not evaluation.
Keep A/B and C separate: in Assignment 1 judge diagnosis and treatment options; save risk and safety evaluation for Assignment 2.
Name the regulations you use (e.g. Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017, IR(ME)R) and check with your tutor that they are current.

AB.D1.decode: Weigh up every ionising and non-ionising option, first for diagnosis then for treatment, for your specific service user, and reach a clear recommendation. The spec expects you to show the physical effect of each on the body at molecular and cellular level.
mustInclude: All the spec techniques considered: laser, MRI, infrared thermography, ultrasound, gamma (external radiotherapy, PET tracers, brachytherapy), X-ray and CT
The physics of each linked to what happens in tissue at molecular and cellular level (e.g. ionisation damaging DNA versus non-ionising heating or vibration)
Diagnosis options judged first, then treatment options, as two clear stages
Strengths and limitations of each option for this service user's condition and medical history
A reasoned recommendation for diagnosis and for treatment, with reasons why the alternatives were rejected
Research evidence or clinical guidance supporting your judgements, referenced
pitfalls: Describing how each machine works with no judgement about the case study
Drifting into risk and side-effect evaluation, which belongs to learning aim C
Recommending a technique without saying why it beats the alternatives
Covering only diagnosis or only treatment
starters: For diagnosing [condition] in [service user],... is more / less suitable than... because...
Although... has the advantage of..., its limitation for this patient is...
Weighing these options, the most appropriate... is... because...
AB.D1.stretch: End with a clear, concise diagnosis-then-treatment pathway that a clinician could act on.

C.D2.decode: Judge how well the health and safety precautions protect both the service user and the operators for each technique used, and how far they reduce the risks and side effects.
mustInclude: Precautions for operators and for service users, treated separately
Ionising precautions: protective clothing, shielding, dose limits, film badges or dosimeters, HSE requirements
MRI precautions: removal of ferromagnetic items, pacemakers, hearing aids, implants, jewellery and piercings
Risks that precautions cannot fully remove (e.g. cumulative dose, cancer risk, unborn and young children, ultrasound probe discomfort)
Strengths and limitations of each precaution, applied to your service user
A supported judgement on how adequate the precautions are overall
pitfalls: Listing precautions without judging how well they work
Forgetting the staff who carry out the procedures
Treating ionising and non-ionising risks as equal
Ignoring the service user's specific circumstances, such as pregnancy or implants
starters: The most effective precaution for operators is... because...
However, this precaution has limits, for example...
Overall, the precautions are adequate / not fully adequate for [service user] because...
C.D2.stretch: Rank the precautions by how much risk each removes, with a reason for each ranking.

C.D3.decode: Give evidence-based reasons why your chosen ionising and non-ionising diagnosis and treatment techniques are right for this service user, once risks, side effects and safety precautions are taken into account. Draw on all three learning aims.
mustInclude: A clearly stated choice of diagnosis and treatment techniques
Benefits of the choice weighed against its risks and side effects for this service user
How safety precautions make the choice acceptable for service user and staff
Why the rejected alternatives carry more risk or less benefit
Research evidence supporting each justification
Concise, professional writing with a firm conclusion
pitfalls: Changing your recommendation from Assignment 1 without explaining why
Justifying with opinion rather than evidence
Ignoring side effects such as tiredness, hair loss or loss of fertility from gamma therapy
starters: My recommendation is [technique] because the benefit of... outweighs the risk of...
This choice is supported by... which shows that...
The risk of... can be reduced by..., which means...
C.D3.stretch: Show how your research changed or confirmed your original recommendation.

22.title: Genetics
22.assignments: Up to two assignments. Assignment 1 covers learning aims A and B (genetics in reproduction, pre- and post-natal factors, AB.D1), usually a case-study report. Assignment 2 covers learning aims C and D (reproductive and gene technologies, legislation and ethics, CD.D2 and D.D3) for a selected individual with a specific genetic disorder.
22.bigIdea: Genes set the starting point, environment shapes the journey, and technology plus law decide which choices people can make. Distinction work connects the science at the cell level to real consequences for one individual and for society.
evidence: Choose your case-study individual and genetic disorder early; every section should come back to them.
Use annotated diagrams for DNA, meiosis, fertilisation and inheritance patterns, then explain them in writing.
Separate genetic (nature) and environmental (nurture) factors, then show how they interact.
Name the regulators and laws in the spec (HFEA, NICE, Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 as amended 2008, Human Rights Act 1998) and check currency with your tutor.
Present ethical arguments from more than one viewpoint before giving your own supported judgement.

AB.D1.decode: Reach reasoned judgements about how much genetics, pre-natal factors and difficulties with reproduction shape post-natal development and care needs across the life course, using a detailed case.
mustInclude: Accurate genetic terminology: genome, genotype, phenotype, chromosomes, DNA
Conception, cell division and chromosomal behaviour from fertilisation to birth
Genetic factors (parental genotype, chromosome disorders such as Down's syndrome) and environmental factors (age, diet, health, drugs, alcohol, poverty, family functioning)
How these factors affect post-natal development and care needs at different life stages
Judgements on which factors matter most and why, including interaction between nature and nurture
Research evidence supporting your judgements
pitfalls: Describing biology without linking it to development or care needs
Listing factors without judging their relative importance
Stopping at birth instead of following effects through the life course
starters: The most significant factor for [individual] is likely to be... because...
While... influences...,... can...
This suggests that care needs in later life may...
AB.D1.stretch: Show how a single genetic or pre-natal factor ripples through several life stages and services.

CD.D2.decode: Weigh up how reproductive and gene technologies improve life chances for your selected individual with a specific genetic disorder and for society, against the ethical challenges they create.
mustInclude: Relevant technologies: screening, assisted reproduction, recombinant DNA, Human Genome Project, gene therapy, genetic modification
Benefits for the individual: psychological wellbeing, quality of life, benefit versus risk
Effects on society: values and beliefs, support systems, resources and cost
Ethical challenges: risk versus benefit, cost to society, pressure groups, enhancement rather than health use
How legislation and regulation limit or enable each technology
A balanced, supported conclusion
pitfalls: Writing generally about technology with no link to your selected disorder
Giving only one side of the ethical debate
Stating laws without explaining their effect on practice
starters: For someone with [disorder], [technology] offers... however...
From society's perspective, an ethical challenge is...
On balance, the benefits outweigh / do not outweigh the challenges because...
CD.D2.stretch: Contrast the individual's view with society's view and explain where they conflict.

D.D3.decode: Judge the overall importance of genetics in pre- and post-natal development and of reproductive and gene technologies in promoting life chances, with ethical challenges in view. This draws the whole unit together.
mustInclude: A synoptic overview linking learning aims A to D
The role of genetics in development, compared with environmental influences
Contribution of technologies to individuals' and society's life chances
How legislation and regulation (HFEA, NICE, relevant Acts) shape what is possible, using research to judge their validity
Key ethical challenges for professionals working with these technologies
A justified overall conclusion on importance
pitfalls: Repeating CD.D2 instead of widening to the whole unit
No overall judgement
Unreferenced claims about future technology
starters: Overall, genetics is most important for... but less decisive for...
Technologies such as... have changed life chances by...
These benefits are affected by..., including...
D.D3.stretch: Make a reasoned prediction about future impact, supported by current research.

23.title: Biomedical Science
23.assignments: Up to two assignments. Assignment 1 covers learning aims A and B (body defences, haematology and blood transfusion, AB.D1). Assignment 2 covers learning aims C and D (cell pathology and biochemistry, CD.D2 and CD.D3), usually a report based on your own research.
23.bigIdea: Laboratories turn samples into decisions: blood, cell and biochemical tests tell clinicians what is wrong and whether treatment is working. Distinction work explains why each test is used and how results combine to reach a diagnosis.
evidence: Always pair a component or system with a disease and the test that detects it; lists of components and diseases on their own do not meet the criteria.
Annotated diagrams can carry structure and function detail, but your judgements must be written.
Focus on the tests and what they look for, not detailed descriptions of analytical equipment.
Cell injury here means damage at cell level (pathogens, abnormal growth, inflammation), not physical injury from a cut or blow.
Use worked examples, such as urine protein levels alongside kidney cell samples, to show tests working together.

AB.D1.decode: Give evidence-based reasons why haematology is so prominent as a diagnostic tool, why blood tests are often the first line of investigation, and why transfusion is prominent in treatment.
mustInclude: Why blood tests are often the first investigation when a patient presents with something abnormal
Haematology tests and what each looks for: blood smears, red cell, reticulocyte and platelet counts, mean corpuscular volume, iron, coagulation, haemoglobin
Links from blood components to diseases (anaemias, thalassaemia, leukaemia, lymphomas, clotting disorders)
Processes that make blood products safe for transfusion: production, red cell compatibility, screening
Clinical uses of blood products, such as surgery, intensive care and inherited conditions
Limitations of screening, including diseases that may not be detected
pitfalls: Writing an account of the blood transfusion service rather than the processes
Describing tests without saying why they are chosen
Unsupported claims with no examples
starters: The first line of investigation for... is... because...
A... test would help diagnose... by showing...
... has a role in treatment because..., although...
AB.D1.stretch: Use a patient pathway example that moves from symptoms to blood test to diagnosis to transfusion.

CD.D2.decode: Judge how effectively cell pathology results, combined with biochemical tests, work as diagnostic tools, using detailed analysis and research.
mustInclude: Cell collection methods: surgical removal, Pap smear, removal of surface cells, aspiration
How cell injury (ageing, neoplasia, lupus, allergic reactions) is identified
Biochemical tests: liver and kidney function, hormone levels, urine and CSF analysis, faecal analysis, toxicology
Worked examples of cell and biochemical results combining to confirm a diagnosis
Strengths and limitations of each approach alone and in combination
A supported judgement on their diagnostic value
pitfalls: Treating cell pathology and biochemistry as separate topics with no link
Only one example
No limitations, such as false results or sampling issues
starters: On its own, a... test showing... suggests..., but combined with... it...
The main strength of... is..., whereas... adds...
The combined approach is most effective when...
CD.D2.stretch: Compare two diseases where combined testing changes the diagnosis or treatment decision.

CD.D3.decode: Judge the work of laboratories in detecting causes and supporting cures of disease, meaning the samples they receive, tests they run and reports they produce for health workers, drawing on your research across the whole unit.
mustInclude: The laboratory process: sample received, tests carried out, report produced for clinicians
Examples from haematology, cell pathology and biochemistry
How lab reports guide diagnosis, treatment and monitoring (e.g. therapeutic drug monitoring)
Strengths and limitations of laboratory work
Justified recommendations or conclusions
Evidence from your own research, referenced
pitfalls: Writing about scientific research rather than diagnostic laboratory work
Ignoring limitations
No conclusion
starters: Laboratories contribute to diagnosis by...
A key limitation of laboratory testing is...
Overall, laboratory work is effective because..., although improvements could include...
CD.D3.stretch: Recommend one realistic improvement to laboratory practice and justify it.

24.title: Biochemistry for Health
24.assignments: Up to three assignments, one per learning aim: A (structure of atoms and molecules, metabolism, A.D1), B (biomolecules, enzymes and nucleic acids with investigations, B.D2) and C (metabolic disorders, biotechnology and research, C.D3).
24.bigIdea: Structure determines function: the way atoms bond decides how molecules behave, which controls metabolic rate and explains metabolic disease. Distinction work traces the chain from atom to molecule to metabolism to disorder to treatment.
evidence: Use your own experimental data from enzyme, food analysis and DNA investigations to support your evaluation.
Include clear diagrams of atoms, bonds and molecules, then explain them in writing.
Link every structure to a function and to metabolism; avoid isolated chemistry facts.
Write investigations as scientific reports: method, results, analysis, limitations, health and safety.
For learning aim C, focus on diabetes and glycogen storage disease as the spec's examples.

A.D1.decode: Judge how the structure, function and role of inorganic and organic molecules affect metabolism, using research and experimental data.
mustInclude: How atomic structure and bonding (covalent, ionic, hydrogen) of C, H, N and O determine molecular properties
Inorganic molecules (water, ions, salts, acids) and their role, including water as solvent and buffer
Organic molecules (proteins, fats, carbohydrates, haemoglobin, membrane proteins, hormones) linked to function
Importance of both anabolism and catabolism
Comparison of aerobic and anaerobic respiration of glucose in terms of oxidation, reduction and energy released
Role of iron ions in oxygen transport and the danger of carbon dioxide if not removed
Experimental data used to support judgements
pitfalls: Describing structures without linking them to metabolism
Going into Krebs cycle detail that the spec says is not required, while missing the comparison of respiration types
Ignoring your experimental evidence
starters: The role of... in metabolism is... because...
Comparing... with..., the difference in energy release is... because...
If my results showed..., this suggests that the structure of...
A.D1.stretch: Explain how a change at atomic or bond level would disrupt a named metabolic process.

B.D2.decode: Judge how the structure, functions and action of biomolecules, especially enzymes such as amylase, affect metabolic rates and can lead to metabolic disease.
mustInclude: Condensation and hydrolysis of organic polymers, glucose metabolism and cellular respiration
Enzyme structure, active site specificity, co-enzymes, co-factors, inhibitors and denaturation
Your investigation results on temperature, pH, concentration and specificity
How factors affecting amylase's action change metabolic rate and could result in metabolic disease
Intermediate molecules such as pyruvate and their relevance to respiration
Nucleic acids and protein synthesis linked to enzyme production
Limitations of your investigations
pitfalls: Reporting results without explaining them using enzyme structure
No link from enzyme activity to metabolic disease
Ignoring errors and reliability in your data
starters: When the... changed, the rate... because the active site...
This matters for metabolism because...
If the activity of... were reduced in the body,... would...
B.D2.stretch: Use your own data to predict the effect of a named inhibitor or condition on metabolism.

C.D3.decode: Judge how the properties and roles of biological molecules shape current research, drug development and treatment of metabolic disorders such as diabetes and glycogen storage disease.
mustInclude: Aetiology of diabetes and glycogen storage disease, including genetic and endocrine causes
How defects in biomolecule structure (e.g. insulin, enzymes) cause the disorder
DNA sequencing, DNA profiling and knowledge of the human genome in developing treatments
Biotechnology uses of enzymes (e.g. streptokinase, glucose isomerase)
Current research and the role of research councils such as BBSRC
Advantages and limitations of these developments, with a supported conclusion
pitfalls: Describing the disorders with no link to biochemistry or research
Out-of-date or unreferenced research claims
No judgement of how far research has improved treatment
starters: Because... is a..., its structure means that...
... has changed treatment of... by...
However, a limit on these advances is...
C.D3.stretch: Evaluate one recent research development and judge its likely impact on patients.

25.title: Complementary Therapies for Health and Social Care
25.assignments: Up to two assignments. Assignment 1 covers learning aim A (types, role and benefits of therapies, A.D1). Assignment 2 covers learning aims B and C (provision alongside conventional treatment, regulation and factors to consider, BC.D2 and BC.D3).
25.bigIdea: Complementary therapies can add real value alongside conventional medicine, but the strength of evidence, regulation and safety vary widely. Distinction work is balanced and evidence-led, neither dismissing nor overselling therapies.
evidence: Match each therapy to a specific service user and disorder rather than writing generally.
Use research evidence (clinical studies, trials, NICE guidance) and note where evidence is weak or missing.
Cover both NHS and private provision, with referral routes and access barriers.
Name professional bodies from the spec (CNHC, FHT, GRCCT, NICE) and check current regulation with your tutor.
Include contraindications, such as pregnancy, prescription medication, diabetes or high blood pressure.

A.D1.decode: Give evidence-based reasons why complementary therapies contribute to maintaining health and wellbeing for service users with different needs, taking a holistic approach.
mustInclude: A range of therapy types: manipulative, touch and massage, natural remedies, holistic, specific therapies
Diagnostic and therapeutic roles, and provision alongside orthodox treatment
Benefits matched to service users with different needs (e.g. pain management, stress, chemotherapy side effects)
Holistic benefits, such as easing a disorder while aiding relaxation
Research evidence supporting the validity of your conclusions
Professional, concise arguments with clear reasons
pitfalls: Claiming benefits without evidence
Describing therapies without linking them to service users
Ignoring the limits of the evidence
starters: For [service user] with [condition], [therapy] is beneficial because...
This is supported / not supported by research showing...
Taking a holistic view, the therapy also...
A.D1.stretch: Distinguish benefits backed by strong evidence from those based mainly on user reports.

BC.D2.decode: Weigh up how complementary therapies are provided in relation to conventional medical treatment, including the factors that must be considered.
mustInclude: NHS and private provision, access and referral systems, service user choice
Factors affecting provision: availability, geography, cost, culture, public attitudes
Therapies alongside conventional treatment for named disorders (musculoskeletal, psychological, cancer, childbirth, etc.)
Research evidence, advantages, disadvantages and contraindications
Controversial issues: safety, unregistered practitioners, lack of scientific evidence
A supported judgement with recommendations justified by research
pitfalls: One-sided writing, either for or against therapies
Describing provision without judging it
Generic examples not tied to a disorder or service user
starters: Provision on the NHS is... because...
Used alongside...,... can..., however...
The strongest argument for / against wider provision is...
BC.D2.stretch: Recommend how provision should change and justify it with evidence and cost.

BC.D3.decode: Judge the overall role of complementary therapies as a service within the health and social care sector, drawing the whole unit together.
mustInclude: Position of complementary therapies in the sector today
Strengths and weaknesses, relevance and significance
Role of regulation, professional bodies, training and codes of ethics
Issues when provided alongside conventional medical treatment
Evidence from across all learning aims
A clear, supported conclusion
pitfalls: Repeating BC.D2 without widening to the whole sector
No conclusion
Ignoring regulation
starters: Overall, complementary therapies play a... role because...
Their value is affected by...
In conclusion, the evidence suggests...
BC.D3.stretch: Judge whether stronger regulation would increase or reduce their role, with reasons.

26.title: Health Psychology
26.assignments: Up to two assignments. Assignment 1 covers learning aims A and B (concepts, influences on beliefs and behaviour, contemporary health issues, AB.D1). Assignment 2 covers learning aims C and D (stress models and strategies, pain and ill health for a selected service user, C.D2 and D.D3).
26.bigIdea: What people believe about health shapes what they do, and psychology offers tools to change behaviour, manage stress and cope with pain. Distinction work applies theory to real issues and a real-feeling service user, then judges what works.
evidence: Name theories and models accurately (health belief model, biopsychosocial model, general adaptation syndrome, life events theory, locus of control).
Apply every theory to an example or your selected service user; theory alone stays at Pass.
Use research to support claims about influences on beliefs and behaviour.
Compare theories: say which explains the issue better and why.
Write about eating disorders and addiction factually and sensitively, using the spec's theoretical focus.

AB.D1.decode: Judge how useful health psychology and concepts of health and ill health are in managing contemporary health issues such as smoking, alcohol, eating behaviour, exercise and childbirth.
mustInclude: Definitions and models: WHO definition, medical model, biopsychosocial model, health belief model, sick role
Influences on beliefs and behaviour: culture, religion, socioeconomic, environmental, individual, education
Application of theory to at least two contemporary issues
Strengths and limitations of each theory or model
Research supporting the validity of influences
A supported judgement on the contribution of health psychology
pitfalls: Describing models without applying them to an issue
No limitations of theories
Treating influences as a list rather than explaining how they shape behaviour
starters: The... model helps explain... because...
However, it does not account for...
Overall, health psychology is most useful for... because...
AB.D1.stretch: Compare how two models would design different interventions for the same issue.

C.D2.decode: Judge how well strategies and psychological theories manage stress, pain and ill health for your selected service user.
mustInclude: Stress models: fight or flight, general adaptation syndrome, life events theory, psychosocial models, locus of control and personality type
Coping strategies: problem-focused, emotion-focused, defence mechanisms, positive and negative coping
The stress-illness link, including effects on the immune system and social support
Theories of pain and psychological approaches to pain control
Application of all of these to the selected service user's situation
Strengths and limitations of each strategy, with a supported conclusion
pitfalls: Generic strategies not tailored to the service user
Covering stress but not pain and ill health
No judgement on which strategies work best
starters: For [service user], a... strategy would... because...
This is likely to be less effective if...
The most suitable approach overall is... because...
C.D2.stretch: Show how strategies should change as the service user's illness or pain progresses.

D.D3.decode: Judge how important health psychology is in helping individuals deal with contemporary health issues, stress, pain and illness, drawing the whole unit together.
mustInclude: Synoptic links across learning aims A to D
Concepts of pain: organic and psychogenic, acute and chronic, referred, measuring pain
Diagnosis and behaviour change, alleviation of symptoms, effects on families and dependants
Examples from illnesses such as heart disease, cancer, HIV/AIDS, back pain or asthma
Importance to professionals of knowing these strategies
Strengths and limitations of health psychology with a clear conclusion
pitfalls: Repeating C.D2 rather than widening to individuals generally
No overall judgement of importance
Ignoring families and dependants
starters: Health psychology contributes by recognising that...
Its contribution is limited where...
On balance, it is most valuable for... because...
D.D3.stretch: Judge the importance of health psychology against purely medical approaches, with evidence.
